passage: The community centre's back room smelled of chalk dust and someone's frying pakoras. Every Saturday, fifteen-year-old Jagdish sat on a plastic stool with three Class 4 kids and a box of bottle caps. "Seven caps, take away three. How many?" Little Preeti counted on her fingers, then shouted, "Four!" and looked at him as if he had invented numbers. Jagdish grinned. At school that week he had come nineteenth in the maths test, and nobody had looked at him at all. Here the kids waited at the door for him, and Preeti's mother had told him, "She talks about Jagdish bhaiya all week." Walking home, he realised he hadn't checked his phone once in two hours.

qa.q: What did Jagdish use to teach subtraction?
qa.a: A box of bottle caps.

qa.q: What does Jagdish not checking his phone for two hours suggest he felt?
qa.a: He felt happy and needed at the centre, in a way he didn't feel at school after coming nineteenth.

qa.q: What choice could help Jagdish keep this sense of worth?
qa.a: He could keep the Saturday sessions going even in exam weeks and value them as much as his test rank.

qa.q: How does Preeti see Jagdish?
qa.a: To her he is someone amazing, as if he had invented numbers; she talks about Jagdish bhaiya all week.

grounding: A teenager who tutors younger children feels needed and valued in a way his test rank never gave him.

passage:
Hi Naveen bhai,
Remember the empty plot behind our building where we used to play? It had turned into a dump. Plastic, broken chairs, a dead scooter. Last month I got fed up and stuck a note in the lift: Sunday 7 am, bring gloves.
I thought five people would come. Twenty-two came, including old Mr D'Souza with his walking stick, handing out bags. We filled forty sacks. The municipal van took them on Monday after Ammi and I called three times.
Here's the weird part. My marks this term are average, and nobody at school notices me. But on Sunday people kept asking, "Farhan, where should this go?" as if I knew. I felt needed. That feeling beats any rank.
We're painting the wall next month. Wish you were here.
Your cousin brother,
Farhan

qa.q: How many people came to the cleanup?
qa.a: Twenty-two came.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel when people kept asking where things should go?
qa.a: Farhan felt needed and trusted, a feeling that beats any rank.

qa.q: What small first step turned Farhan's frustration into action?
qa.a: A note in the lift with a time and a simple ask, bring gloves, which made it easy for neighbours to join.

qa.q: How might Mr D'Souza have felt joining the cleanup?
qa.a: He may have felt useful and part of the neighbourhood again, handing out bags despite his walking stick 😊

grounding: A teenager organises a neighbourhood cleanup and feels needed in a way average marks never gave him.

passage: Why do I coach the under-tens, Sabina? Honestly, it started because my cousin dumped the job on me. I'm a very average midfielder. I've never been picked for district. But on the first evening at the park, a tiny kid called Moinak cried because he kept missing the ball. I showed him to watch the ball, not his feet, and twenty minutes later he scored into the empty goal and ran round the whole park screaming. I was screaming too. Now twelve kids wait for me every Tuesday and Thursday. If I'm late, they phone my mum. At school I'm roll number 23. At the park I'm Karthik anna. That's a different feeling. My marks didn't change. I did.

qa.q: What did Karthik show Moinak?
qa.a: To watch the ball, not his feet.

qa.q: What is Karthik feeling when he says, "My marks didn't change. I did"?
qa.a: He feels a new sense of worth from being needed at the park, something his average marks and roll number never gave him.

qa.q: Which moment was the turning point for Karthik, and why?
qa.a: When Moinak scored after his tip and they both screamed; it showed Karthik he could make a real difference, so he kept coming.

qa.q: How might Moinak have felt when he scored into the empty goal?
qa.a: Moinak probably felt thrilled and proud after crying over missed balls, which is why he ran round the whole park screaming.

grounding: A teenager who coaches younger children finds a sense of worth in being needed that grades and status did not give.

passage:
I'm Anirban, Dolma's cousin, and I live two floors above her in our Darjeeling colony. I can't tell you what goes on inside her, only what I've seen. At school Dolma is middling: average marks, not on any team, the kind of girl teachers forget to name.
Last winter she cleared out the empty garage behind Block C, borrowed a mat and a crate of old picture books, and put up a sign: Saturday Story Corner, ages 4 to 8. By March there were eleven kids. Little Karma now waits at the gate at nine.
I've watched her read the same bear book three times in a row without sighing. She kneels to tie shoelaces and remembers every child's name. When she walks home afterwards, she stands straighter than she does on report-card day.

qa.q: What sign did Dolma put up?
qa.a: Saturday Story Corner, ages 4 to 8.

qa.q: What might Dolma's straighter walk home suggest, even though Anirban can't be sure?
qa.a: It suggests she feels proud and valued, since being needed by the children gives her a sense of worth her average marks don't.

qa.q: What choice turned an empty garage into something meaningful?
qa.a: Dolma chose to clear it out and start the story corner, turning her Saturdays into something useful to others.

qa.q: What might the Story Corner mean to little Karma?
qa.a: It may be the best part of Karma's week, with someone who knows Karma's name and reads patiently.

grounding: A cousin observes a teenager with average marks who starts a story corner for small children and seems to find a sense of worth in being needed.

passage:
Monday. Parveen, fifteen, didn't make the school quiz team, again. That evening she signed up as a helper at the Saturday maths club for the government primary school down the road, mainly to stop thinking about it.
Saturday. She sat on a bench with Ujjwal, nine, who hid his notebook whenever fractions came up. She cut a roti-sized circle of paper into halves, then quarters. On the third try Ujjwal said, "Oh! So a quarter is smaller than a half even though four is bigger!" and looked at her as if she'd done magic.
A month later. Her report card was ordinary. She noticed she didn't mind as much. On Saturday Ujjwal came running, notebook open, to show her a sum with a red tick.

qa.q: What did Parveen cut into halves and then quarters?
qa.a: A roti-sized circle of paper.

qa.q: Why did Parveen mind her ordinary report card less a month later?
qa.a: She felt less disappointed, because being needed by Ujjwal gave her a sense of worth that marks and the quiz team didn't.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Parveen at the maths club?
qa.a: When Ujjwal finally understood quarters and looked at her as if she'd done magic, showing her she was really useful.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel running to show Parveen his red tick?
qa.a: He likely feels proud and eager to share it with the person who helped him understand. 🎉

grounding: After missing the quiz team, a teenager helps younger children with maths and finds a sense of worth in being needed that grades did not give.

passage: Okay, so the principal asked me to say something for the school radio. Hi, I'm Sharmila, class ten. Every evening at six, I teach maths to five kids in our building's parking lot. It started because Pranav, he's in class four, was crying on the stairs about fractions. I showed him with a roti, halves and quarters. Next day his friend came. Then three more. I don't get paid. I'm not a topper; I got sixty-eight in my own maths test. But when Pranav got full marks in his class test, he ran down with the paper waving, shouting my name. I have never felt that at any prize ceremony. At home I'm just the middle child who gets told to study harder. Down there on that cold parking floor, people actually need me. That's all. Thank you for listening.

qa.q: How many kids does Sharmila teach in the parking lot?
qa.a: Sharmila teaches maths to five kids.

qa.q: Why does the parking lot matter so much to Sharmila?
qa.a: There Sharmila feels needed, useful and proud, which gives a sense of worth that grades and prize ceremonies never did.

qa.q: What could the school do to support students like Sharmila?
qa.a: The school could recognise tutoring as real contribution and give students like Sharmila a quiet room or materials, without turning it into a competition.

qa.q: How did Sharmila's help affect Pranav?
qa.a: Pranav went from crying on the stairs about fractions to full marks, and ran down excited, showing he felt proud and grateful.

grounding: A teenager tutors younger children in the building and feels needed, finding a worth that grades and status never gave.

passage:
First Sunday: The lane behind Asif's building in Lucknow had become a dump: chip packets, broken slippers, a dead scooter. Asif, fifteen, stuck a handwritten notice on the lamp post: CLEANUP SUNDAY 8 AM. Only Preeti from the third floor turned up. They filled four sacks and felt a bit foolish.
Second Sunday: Nine people came, including two aunties with brooms and the watchman. Someone brought chai. Asif found himself directing who swept where, surprised that grown-ups listened.
Fourth Sunday: The municipal van came because Preeti had emailed the ward office. Little kids now drew chalk hopscotch on the clean patch. Mrs Verma, who never smiled, told Asif, "You've done something here." He had scored badly in his chemistry test that week. Somehow, it didn't sting as much.

qa.q: How many people came on the second Sunday?
qa.a: Nine people came on the second Sunday.

qa.q: What did Asif feel on the first Sunday, when only Preeti came?
qa.a: Asif felt a bit foolish and discouraged, unsure the cleanup would catch on.

qa.q: What small step helped the cleanup grow, and why?
qa.a: Preeti emailed the ward office, which brought the municipal van and showed neighbours the effort was being taken seriously.

qa.q: How might the little kids drawing hopscotch see the lane now?
qa.a: For the little kids the lane is now a safe, clean place to play, which they may not have had before.

grounding: Over weeks, a teenager organises a neighbourhood cleanup and feels needed, finding a worth that a poor test mark cannot take away.

passage: Damini, you think your weekend tutoring is small? Let me tell you about the flood summer. I'm Noor, and I was fourteen when the river came into our basti in Srinagar. School was shut for two months. The little ones were running wild in the mud, forgetting even their alphabet. My mother said, "You know your letters, teach them." So I did, on the steps of the mosque, with a slate and chalk. Nine children, then fifteen. My own marks that year were terrible. Nobody gave me a certificate. But one boy, Bilal, read his first full sentence aloud and the whole step clapped, and I felt taller than I have ever felt since. Years later that boy became a schoolteacher. So no, Damini, it is not small. Being needed is its own kind of worth.

qa.q: Where did Noor teach the children?
qa.a: Noor taught them on the steps of the mosque, with a slate and chalk.

qa.q: How did Noor feel when Bilal read his first full sentence?
qa.a: Noor felt enormously proud and needed, taller than ever since, even though no certificate came.

qa.q: Why was agreeing to teach the little ones a turning point for Noor in the story?
qa.a: It gave Noor a sense of worth during a year of terrible marks, and it helped children who were losing their learning.

qa.q: How might Bilal have felt when the whole step clapped?
qa.a: Bilal probably felt proud and encouraged, perhaps the first seed of wanting to teach others himself.

grounding: An elder recalls teaching younger children as a teenager after a flood and finding a worth that marks and certificates never gave.

passage:
The board exams were two months away, and Dilnaz, sixteen, had her own studies piling up. But every Tuesday she still walked to the community centre in her Hyderabad basti to tutor three Class 5 girls in maths.
This week the power was out and they worked by a phone torch. Irawati, the smallest, finally understood fractions. She jumped up. "Didi, I get it!"
Dilnaz felt something warm spread through her chest. At school she was just another roll number, never topping anything. Here, someone needed her.
Walking home in the dark, she thought, marks don't make me feel like this.

qa.q: What did Irawati finally understand?
qa.a: She finally understood fractions.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz feel when Irawati understood?
qa.a: She felt warm and proud, needed in a way she never felt from marks at school.

qa.q: How could Dilnaz balance tutoring with exam preparation?
qa.a: Keep the weekly Tuesday session, since it gives her worth, while planning study time around it.

qa.q: How might Irawati see Dilnaz?
qa.a: Irawati probably admires her and feels grateful, calling her Didi and jumping with joy.

grounding: A teenager tutors younger girls despite her own exams and feels a worth that marks don't give her.

passage:
Jomon, fifteen, was not a topper and not a sports star at his school in Kochi. But when his neighbour Gautam, a retired teacher, asked for help organising the colony's monsoon cleanup, Jomon said yes.
He made posters. He knocked on every door. On Sunday he handed out gloves and bags to twenty neighbours, directed the little kids to pick up plastic, and helped clear the blocked drain near the temple.
By noon the lane was clean. Gautam shook his hand. "You organised this better than I could."
Jomon grinned all the way home. Nobody at school had ever said anything like that. He felt, for the first time in months, like he mattered.

qa.q: How many neighbours did Jomon hand gloves and bags to?
qa.a: He handed them to twenty neighbours.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel walking home after the cleanup?
qa.a: He felt proud and happy, feeling like he mattered for the first time in months.

qa.q: What could Jomon do to keep this sense of worth?
qa.a: Keep volunteering in ways that use his organising skills, like future cleanups or helping neighbours.

qa.q: How does Gautam see Jomon's work?
qa.a: Gautam is impressed, saying Jomon organised it better than he could.

grounding: A teenager who isn't a topper organises a neighbourhood cleanup and feels a worth that grades and status never gave him.

passage:
"Sudha, why are you always at the library on Saturdays?" asked her friend Ganga.
"I help the little kids with reading."
"For free? When you could be at the mall?"
Sudha laughed. "It's the best part of my week."
"Why?"
"At school I'm average. Nobody notices me. But yesterday, a Class 2 boy read a whole page aloud for the first time. He looked at me like I'd given him the moon."
Ganga was quiet. "That sounds nice."
"It is. I feel useful. Like I'm actually good for something."
"Can I come next week?"
"Only if you're ready to read about dinosaurs forty times."

qa.q: What did the Class 2 boy do for the first time?
qa.a: He read a whole page aloud for the first time.

qa.q: How does Sudha feel when she helps the little kids?
qa.a: She feels useful and proud, noticed in a way she isn't at school.

qa.q: Why is helping at the library good for Sudha, beyond grades?
qa.a: It gives her a sense of worth and being needed that being average at school doesn't.

qa.q: How does Ganga's view of Sudha's Saturdays change?
qa.a: Ganga first wonders why she'd do it for free, then sees it's meaningful and asks to come along.

grounding: A teenager helps young children read and feels a worth and usefulness that grades and status don't give her.

passage: Last summer I started teaching maths to kids in the lane behind our building, mostly because Ammi wouldn't stop nagging me to do something useful. I'm Wasim, and honestly I thought it would be boring. Then I met Vijay, nine, who couldn't do subtraction and said he was 'dumb, everyone says'. We used marbles. We used cricket scores. On the fourteenth day he got a whole page right and threw his pencil in the air. I've topped tests before and felt nothing much. That day I walked home feeling like I actually mattered to someone. Now when my marks slip, it doesn't wreck me the same way, because on Tuesday and Thursday evenings there's a kid waiting for me with a sharpened pencil.

qa.q: What did Wasim use to teach Vijay?
qa.a: Marbles and cricket scores.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel walking home on the fourteenth day?
qa.a: Wasim felt proud and needed, as if truly mattering to someone, more than after topping tests.

qa.q: How could Wasim keep this going after the summer?
qa.a: Wasim could keep the Tuesday and Thursday sessions and perhaps bring a friend to teach other kids in the lane.

qa.q: What might the sessions mean to Vijay?
qa.a: Vijay, who thought he was dumb, may feel capable and cared for, proud enough to throw his pencil in the air.

grounding: A teenager tutoring a younger child finds a sense of worth that grades never gave.

passage:
Scout leader's note, Sunday beach clean-up, Vasco.
Thomas organised this entirely. He made the posters, got the colony secretary to lend gloves and sacks, and persuaded Chinmay and six others to come at 7 am. By 9 we had filled nineteen sacks, mostly plastic and fishing line. What struck me was how Thomas changed as the morning went on. He usually hangs back in troop meetings and says little. Today he was directing, joking, thanking each volunteer by name. When an old fisherman thanked him for clearing the net area, Thomas went red and grinned for a long time. Chinmay told me Thomas's marks have been low this term and he has been down about it. Next: I've asked Thomas to plan a monthly clean-up, with Chinmay as co-organiser.

qa.q: How many sacks did they fill by 9?
qa.a: Nineteen sacks, mostly plastic and fishing line.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel when the fisherman thanked him?
qa.a: Thomas felt proud and a little shy, going red and grinning for a long time.

qa.q: Why is asking Thomas to plan a monthly clean-up a good next step?
qa.a: It builds on the worth he found in being useful, especially when low marks have left him feeling down.

qa.q: How might Chinmay see Thomas that morning?
qa.a: Chinmay probably sees a more confident Thomas than usual, which matters to a friend who knew he had been feeling low.

grounding: A scout leader notes a quiet teenager organising a beach clean-up and finding worth in being useful.

passage:
Saturday.
Today was the first day of the colony book corner!! Omkar from B-block, the shy one who's seven, came first and wouldn't leave. I'd spent two weekends collecting old books from every flat and painting the shelf in the watchman's room. Mummy thought it was a waste of revision time. But when Omkar read a whole page aloud to me and then looked up to check I was proud, something went warm in my chest. I got 71 in chemistry last week and cried over it. Today I didn't think about marks once. Aunties kept stopping by to say thank you. I'm tired, there's paint on my elbow, and I feel more like me than I have all term.
Binita

qa.q: Where was the book corner's shelf painted?
qa.a: In the watchman's room.

qa.q: What did Binita feel when Omkar looked up after reading?
qa.a: Binita felt warm and proud, a sense of being needed that marks never gave.

qa.q: What small step could make the book corner last?
qa.a: Binita could ask a couple of friends or aunties to take turns running it, so it keeps going during exams.

qa.q: How might Omkar feel about the book corner?
qa.a: Omkar, usually shy, probably feels welcome and proud, checking that Binita is proud of the reading.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows starting a neighbourhood book corner and feeling a worth that marks do not give.
